Experiments that changed questions

The still face: two minutes without a response

When a mother stops responding, the baby tries to win her back, and if that fails, becomes distressed. What matters is the repair.

In 1975, the psychologist Edward Tronick presented a simple experiment. A mother plays face to face with her baby of a few months. Then, for about two minutes, she keeps her face blank and stops responding, while still looking at the baby. Then she plays normally again.

What the baby does

At first the baby smiles, points or makes sounds to regain her attention. When that fails, the baby looks away, slumps, cries or loses postural control. When the interaction returns, the baby calms down, though sometimes not right away.

The experiment shows that babies are active participants in the relationship, not passive recipients. Tronick stressed that what matters is not that caregivers always respond perfectly, which is impossible, but repair: ordinary interactions are full of mismatches, and learning that they get put right helps babies regulate their emotions.

References

  1. Tronick, E. et al. (1978). The infant's response to entrapment between contradictory messages in face-to-face interaction. Journal of the American Academy of Child Psychiatry, 17(1), 1–13.
  2. Tronick, E. y Gold, C. (2020). The Power of Discord. Little, Brown Spark.
